english.html: the intention of enriching oneself, or of harming one's neighbour e. I have excepted only Draco, the ancient legislator of Athens, who by his cruel and bloody laws put all criminals to death indifferently, and singularly thieves, even supposing they had stolen but a mere pennyworth of herbs f. Nevertheless, inasmuch as he appointed one and the same penalty for all misdeeds, however small they were, even to punishing with death a little idleness and sloth, all these laws, which Demades used to say had been written in blood and not in ink, were, as barbarous and inhuman, removed and abolished, or at the least, by a tacit consent of the Athenians, consigned to oblivion; one alone excepted, by which murderers were condemned to death g. But thefts which are atrocious, and qualified by some notable gravity, must also be more grievously and severely punished h, and sometimes even to death, whether civil or natural i: as are the sacrilegious, despoilers, diaetarii [chamber-thieves], and breakers of the peace k. Among all of whom our rustic du Tilh will readily find a place. For in the first place he is sacrilegious, as has been shown above l. Next, he is a despoiler, having left nothing of Martin Guerre's property unstolen m. Further, he is a diaetarius, or as others read, a directarius, having taken possession by stealth and by treachery not only of a chamber, to rob it, but of the whole house n. He is moreover a breaker of the peace, and so punishable with death, were the theft but of five sols o — the more so in this case, where it is a question of having troubled a peaceable and well-accorded marriage, which is a violation and great rupture of a commendable public peace and tranquillity p, and which the laws have ordained to be grievously and severely punished, even though no act of lechery should have followed from it q.

notes.citation: Decretals, X 5.18 (De furtis), c. Si quis propter necessitatem (X 5.18.3)
notes.original: c. ſi quis ꝓ pter neceſsita tem de fur.
notes.gloss: One who steals food, clothing or a beast for hunger or nakedness does penance for three weeks and, if he can, makes restitution — theft from necessity lightly punished. The ꝓ is the pro- sign: propter. The print's c. is capitulum; see the report on the `⟨alt⟩`.

notes.citation: Gellius, Attic Nights, book 11, c. 18 (§ 3: Draco punished every theft with death, even of vegetables or fruit)

Gellius, Attic Nights, book 11, c. 18, as above (§§ 4–5: Draco's laws fell into disuse by the tacit, unwritten consent of the Athenians, save the law on homicide); the saying of Demades is in Plutarch, Solon, c. 17

notes.original: l. ſaccularij. D. de extract. crim.
notes.gloss: Purse-snatchers (saccularii) and directarii — those who make their way into other men's rooms to steal — are to be punished more than ordinary thieves, by condemnation to the mines or by relegation according to the person. The print's de extract. crim. is de extraord. crim.
